lesson.title: The idea: why PCA chases variance
lesson.lead: Explained as if you are 10, then on the slides' maths. `Lecture_12.pdf` p. 2–8.

blocks.text: **Picture it.** You have a cloud of dots on paper. You may keep only **one number** per dot instead of two. So you draw a line, drop each dot straight onto it (its **shadow**), and keep only where the shadow lands. Which line loses the least? The one where the shadows are **most spread out**, because spread-out shadows still tell the dots apart. Shadows bunched together lose almost everything.

**Spread = variance.** So PCA's question is: which direction makes the shadows' variance as large as possible? That direction is the **first principal component (PC1)**. The second (PC2) is the best direction at right angles to PC1, and so on.

items: Turn the line: the spread V(θ) on the right goes up and down.
Its highest point is **λ₁** and happens exactly along the top eigenvector of S. Its lowest point is **λ₂**, exactly 90° away.
So "the line with the biggest spread" and "the eigenvector of the biggest eigenvalue" are the same thing. Lecture 12 proves this with a Lagrangian.

lesson.title: Type 1 · Full PCA by hand: the recipe
lesson.lead: Mar 2026 Q5, Practice Paper Q5, Sep 2025 Q2(b), and every older paper. `Lecture_12.pdf` p. 25–27, `Lecture_13.pdf` p. 17–23.

groups.label: 2 · Centre
groups.note: X̂ = the centred points as rows (N × D). Check: each column of X̂ adds to 0.

groups.label: 3 · Covariance matrix
groups.note: Divide by **N, never N − 1**, in this course. Saurabh sir calls this matrix C. With 3 features S is 3 × 3: also s₃₃, s₁₃, s₂₃.

groups.label: 4 · Eigenvalues (first line works for any size)
groups.note: Sort them: λ₁ ≥ λ₂. Check: λ₁ + λ₂ = tr S and λ₁λ₂ = det S.

groups.label: 5 · Unit eigenvectors
groups.note: PC1 = b₁ for λ₁. In 2-D, PC2 = b₂ is perpendicular: swap the two numbers and change one sign. Check: b₁ · b₂ = 0. (Quick form needs s₁₂ ≠ 0; if s₁₂ = 0 the PCs are the axes.)

groups.label: 6 · Scores (project the centred points)
groups.note: Check: the scores add to 0, and (1/N) Σ z₁ₙ² = λ₁. Find z₂ₙ = b₂ᵀ(xₙ − μ) only if asked.

groups.label: 7 · Share of variance and how many to keep
groups.note: Keep PC1, PC2, … until the running total reaches what the question asks (90% or 95%).

blocks.label: Where marks are lost
blocks.text: **Not centring** before S · dividing by **N − 1** (this course uses 1/N) · an eigenvector that is **not unit length** · picking the **smaller** λ · not sorting λ₁ ≥ λ₂ · projecting raw points instead of centred ones (the scores then shift by a constant) · not writing the share as a %.

lesson.title: Type 2 · Why PC1 is an eigenvector: the Lagrangian proof
lesson.lead: `Lecture_12.pdf` p. 9–23. Same Lagrange method as Lecture 11.

blocks.text: Exactly as he did it in the 14 Nov class (and Companion §4). Write it in this order in the exam.

blocks.label: Write this line first
blocks.text: **Assumptions:** X is the N × D data matrix, one data point per row, already centred (mean 0). w is a D × 1 unit vector (wᵀw = 1). z = Xw are the projections of the N points onto w. C = (1/N)XᵀX is the covariance matrix (divide by N, not N − 1).

groups.label: 1 · Project the data onto a direction w (dot product)
lines: xᵢᵀw   (one point, row i of X)
groups.note: Centre first so every direction is measured from the origin. Only the direction of w matters, not its length, so take ‖w‖ = 1.

groups.label: 2 · Variance of the projected data
groups.note: XᵀX / N is the covariance matrix C: this is why PCA uses it, it appears by itself once the data is centred. Divide by N, never N − 1, in this course.

groups.label: 5 · Differentiate with respect to w and set to 0
groups.note: C is symmetric, so ∂(wᵀCw)/∂w = 2Cw; and ∂(wᵀw)/∂w = 2w. Cw = λw is the eigenvector equation: the best direction w is an **eigenvector of C**, and the multiplier λ is its **eigenvalue**.

groups.label: 6 · The maximum variance is λ
groups.note: So pick the eigenvector with the **largest** λ: that is PC1. Last year's paper asked exactly these two things: show w is an eigenvector, and show the maximum variance is λ.

groups.label: 7 · More than one direction, and the share of variance
groups.note: W holds the unit eigenvectors, largest λ first; column k of Z is the data projected on wₖ. Keep components until the share reaches what the question asks (90% or 95%).

groups.label: 8 · The components are uncorrelated (asked as "correlation between Y₁ and Y₂")
groups.note: w₁ᵀw₂ = 0 because C is symmetric, so its eigenvectors are perpendicular. Example: [P41 (d)](#/sem1/aiml-zc416/ch12/f-derive/12): α₁ = (2, 1)/√5, α₂ = (1, −2)/√5 ⇒ α₁ᵀα₂ = (2 − 2)/5 = 0 ⇒ correlation 0.

blocks.label: About the sign
blocks.text: In class he wrote L = wᵀCw **+** λ(wᵀw − 1). Differentiating gives Cw = −λw, and he then renamed −λ as a new letter. Writing **− λ(wᵀw − 1)**, as above, gives Cw = λw straight away. Both earn the marks.

blocks.label: Notation rule (Saurabh sir, 14 Nov)
blocks.text: If the question gives letters (Z = XW, α, b₁…), **use the question's letters** and change the assumption line to match. If it gives none, use the line above. Never mix two notations in one answer.
`Lecture_12.pdf` p. 9–23, in the slides' letters: b₁ for the direction, S for the covariance matrix.

groups.label: Constrained problem
groups.note: Without the constraint, a longer b₁ gives a bigger number forever: only the direction should count.

groups.label: Lagrangian
groups.note: So b₁ must be an eigenvector of S, and λ (the multiplier) is its eigenvalue.

groups.label: Which eigenvector
groups.note: The variance along an eigenvector equals its eigenvalue, so take the **largest** λ.

groups.label: M components
lines: [b₁ b₂ … ] : the eigenvectors of the M largest λ
groups.note: Each next PC is the best direction perpendicular to the ones already chosen; S is symmetric, so its eigenvectors are perpendicular (spectral theorem).

groups.label: Uncorrelated components
groups.note: So the correlation between any two PCs is 0.

blocks.text: **Why ∇f = λ∇g (p. 14–15):** at the best point on the circle ‖b‖ = 1, moving along the circle cannot improve f, so ∇f has no part along the circle. ∇g is also perpendicular to the circle. Two vectors perpendicular to the same direction (in 2-D) are parallel: ∇f = λ∇g.

worked.title: Full PCA · Mar 2026 Q5: covariance, eigenvectors, principal subspace (7 marks)

problem.text: Rows are observations: X = [[0, 3], [1, 5], [2, 7]]. (1) Compute the covariance matrix S. [2M] (2) Find the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of S. [3M] (3) Find the 1-dimensional principal subspace. [2M]

steps.label: What is tested
steps.text: The full PCA recipe on three 2-D points: centre → S → eigen → pick the largest. Marks 2 + 3 + 2.

steps.label: Plan of attack
steps.text:
1. Mean of each column, subtract it.
2. S = (1/N)X_cᵀX_c.
3. det(S − λI) = 0, then (S − λI)v = 0 for each λ.
4. The eigenvector of the largest λ spans the principal subspace.

steps.label: Notation
steps.text: This paper's symbols are kept. **S** (or **Σ**, **C**) = covariance matrix, **λ** = an eigenvalue of S (**not** a Lagrange multiplier here), **v**, **q**, **α**, **b**, **e** = a unit eigenvector = a principal direction, **z** = a point's score (its coordinate along the direction).

steps.label: STEP 3 · Covariance  [2M]
steps.text:
Saurabh sir's method: **S = (1/N) X̂ᵀX̂**, N = 3
X̂ = [[−1, −2], [0, 0], [1, 2]]   (3 × 2, one centred point per row)
X̂ᵀ = [[−1, 0, 1], [−2, 0, 2]]   (2 × 3: row 1 = feature 1, row 2 = feature 2)
X̂ᵀX̂: each entry = a row of X̂ᵀ times a column of X̂, multiply in pairs and add
top-left (feature 1 · feature 1) = (−1)(−1) + (0)(0) + (1)(1) = 1 + 0 + 1 = 2
top-right (feature 1 · feature 2) = (−1)(−2) + (0)(0) + (1)(2) = 2 + 0 + 2 = 4
bottom-left = top-right = 4 (symmetric)
bottom-right (feature 2 · feature 2) = (−2)(−2) + (0)(0) + (2)(2) = 4 + 0 + 4 = 8
X̂ᵀX̂ = [[2, 4], [4, 8]]
S = (1/3)·[[2, 4], [4, 8]] = **[[2/3, 4/3], [4/3, 8/3]]**
Divide by N, not N − 1 (this course).
The answer key also accepts 1/(N − 1) = 1/2, giving [[1, 2], [2, 4]], but stick to 1/N.

steps.label: STEP 6 · Principal subspace  [2M]
steps.text:
Largest eigenvalue 10/3 ⇒ **span{(1, 2)}**, the line through the mean in direction (1, 2).
λ₂ = 0: all three points lie exactly on that line, so PC1 keeps 100% of the variance.
Scores (centred) along (1, 2)/√5: −√5, 0, √5.

steps.label: Where marks are lost
steps.text:
• Not centring before building S.
• Picking the eigenvector of λ = 0.
• Not saying which divisor (1/N or 1/(N − 1)) you used.

worked.title: Full PCA · Practice Paper Q5: scores and explained variance (6 marks)

problem.text: Points (2, 0), (0, 2), (3, 3), (−1, −1); use S = (1/N)X_cᵀX_c. (a) Mean and X_c. [1M] (b) S. [1M] (c) Eigenvalues and unit eigenvectors. [2M] (d) The first PC, the scores zₙ, and the fraction of variance it explains. [2M]

steps.label: What is tested
steps.text: The same recipe, plus scores and the explained share.

steps.label: Plan of attack
steps.text: Centre → S → eigen (trace and determinant) → unit PC1 → scores zₙ = q₁ᵀ(xₙ − x̄) → λ₁/(λ₁ + λ₂).

steps.label: Notation
steps.text: This paper's symbols are kept. **S** (or **Σ**, **C**) = covariance matrix, **λ** = an eigenvalue of S (**not** a Lagrange multiplier here), **v**, **q**, **α**, **b**, **e** = a unit eigenvector = a principal direction, **z** = a point's score (its coordinate along the direction).

steps.label: STEP 2 · (b) S  [1M]
steps.text:
Saurabh sir's method: **S = (1/N) X̂ᵀX̂**, N = 4
X̂ = [[1, −1], [−1, 1], [2, 2], [−2, −2]]   (4 × 2, one centred point per row)
X̂ᵀ = [[1, −1, 2, −2], [−1, 1, 2, −2]]   (2 × 4: row 1 = feature 1, row 2 = feature 2)
X̂ᵀX̂: each entry = a row of X̂ᵀ times a column of X̂, multiply in pairs and add
top-left (feature 1 · feature 1) = (1)(1) + (−1)(−1) + (2)(2) + (−2)(−2) = 1 + 1 + 4 + 4 = 10
top-right (feature 1 · feature 2) = (1)(−1) + (−1)(1) + (2)(2) + (−2)(−2) = −1 − 1 + 4 + 4 = 6
bottom-left = top-right = 6 (symmetric)
bottom-right (feature 2 · feature 2) = (−1)(−1) + (1)(1) + (2)(2) + (−2)(−2) = 1 + 1 + 4 + 4 = 10
X̂ᵀX̂ = [[10, 6], [6, 10]]
S = (1/4)·[[10, 6], [6, 10]] = **[[5/2, 3/2], [3/2, 5/2]]**
Divide by N, not N − 1 (this course).

steps.label: STEP 4 · (c) Unit eigenvectors  [1M]
steps.text:
Formula: **(S − λI)v = 0** for each λ, with v = (v₁, v₂). Solving row 1 is enough: when λ is right, row 2 gives the same line.
**λ₁ = 4:**
S − 4I = [[−3/2, 3/2], [3/2, −3/2]]
row 1: −(3/2)v₁ + (3/2)v₂ = 0 ⇒ v₂ = v₁
row 2: (3/2)v₁ − (3/2)v₂ = 0 ⇒ the same line ✓
⇒ (1, 1); length √(1² + 1²) = √2 ⇒ **q₁ = (1, 1)/√2**
**λ₂ = 1:**
S − I = [[3/2, 3/2], [3/2, 3/2]]
row 1: (3/2)v₁ + (3/2)v₂ = 0 ⇒ v₂ = −v₁
row 2: (3/2)v₁ + (3/2)v₂ = 0 ⇒ the same line ✓
⇒ (1, −1); length √(1² + (−1)²) = √2 ⇒ **q₂ = (1, −1)/√2**
Check: q₁ · q₂ = 0, perpendicular ✓

steps.label: Where marks are lost
steps.text:
• Building S from un-centred data.
• Mixing 1/N and 1/(N − 1).
• Giving (1, 1) instead of the unit vector (1, 1)/√2.

worked.title: Full PCA · Sep 2025 Q2(b): covariance and the direction of maximum variance (3 marks)

problem.text: A = [[−2, 0], [1, 1], [1, −1]]. Treat the rows of A as sample data. Find the eigenvalues of the covariance matrix and the direction of maximum variance. [3M]

steps.label: What is tested
steps.text: Reading PCA off data that is already centred and gives a diagonal covariance.

steps.label: Plan of attack
steps.text: Check the mean → AᵀA → divide → eigenvalues straight off the diagonal → the axis of the bigger one.

steps.label: Notation
steps.text: This paper's symbols are kept. **S** (or **Σ**, **C**) = covariance matrix, **λ** = an eigenvalue of S (**not** a Lagrange multiplier here), **v**, **q**, **α**, **b**, **e** = a unit eigenvector = a principal direction, **z** = a point's score (its coordinate along the direction).

steps.label: STEP 1 · Mean
steps.text: Column 1: (−2 + 1 + 1)/3 = 0; column 2: (0 + 1 − 1)/3 = 0 ⇒ already centred.

steps.label: STEP 2 · Covariance
steps.text:
Saurabh sir's method: **S = (1/N) AᵀA**, N = 3
A = [[−2, 0], [1, 1], [1, −1]]   (3 × 2, already centred)
Aᵀ = [[−2, 1, 1], [0, 1, −1]]   (2 × 3: row 1 = feature 1, row 2 = feature 2)
AᵀA: each entry = a row of Aᵀ times a column of A, multiply in pairs and add
top-left (feature 1 · feature 1) = (−2)(−2) + (1)(1) + (1)(1) = 4 + 1 + 1 = 6
top-right (feature 1 · feature 2) = (−2)(0) + (1)(1) + (1)(−1) = 0 + 1 − 1 = 0
bottom-left = top-right = 0 (symmetric)
bottom-right (feature 2 · feature 2) = (0)(0) + (1)(1) + (−1)(−1) = 0 + 1 + 1 = 2
AᵀA = [[6, 0], [0, 2]]
With 1/N (Saurabh sir's rule): S = (1/3)·[[6, 0], [0, 2]] = **[[2, 0], [0, 2/3]]**
The answer key divides by N − 1 = 2 because the question says "sample": S = **[[3, 0], [0, 1]]**. The next step uses the key's numbers; the direction is the same either way.

steps.label: STEP 3 · Eigenvalues and direction
steps.text:
Formula: **det(S − λI) = 0** (S = [[3, 0], [0, 1]] as in the key)
S − λI = [[3 − λ, 0], [0, 1 − λ]]
det = (3 − λ)(1 − λ) − 0·0 = 0 ⇒ **λ₁ = 3, λ₂ = 1** (with 1/N: 2 and 2/3)
Formula: **(S − λI)v = 0**
**λ₁ = 3:** S − 3I = [[0, 0], [0, −2]] ⇒ row 2: −2v₂ = 0 ⇒ v₂ = 0, v₁ free ⇒ **(1, 0)**
**λ₂ = 1:** S − I = [[2, 0], [0, 0]] ⇒ row 1: 2v₁ = 0 ⇒ v₁ = 0, v₂ free ⇒ **(0, 1)**
(Here row 1 alone says nothing for λ₁, so use the row that is not all zeros.)
The largest λ belongs to (1, 0) ⇒ maximum variance along the **x₁-axis, direction (1, 0)**.
Shortcut: a diagonal matrix's eigenvalues are its diagonal entries, and its eigenvectors are the axes.

steps.label: Answers at a glance
steps.text: Covariance [[3, 0], [0, 1]] (1/(N − 1)); eigenvalues 3, 1; direction (1, 0).

steps.label: Where marks are lost
steps.text:
• Forgetting to check (or state) that the mean is already 0.
• Not saying which divisor you used.

steps.label: More
steps.text: Full question with the SVD part: [Exam hall · Sep 2025 Q2](#/sem1/aiml-zc416/p-es-reg-2025/worked/2).

worked.answer: Eigenvalues 3 and 1; maximum variance along (1, 0). (Side note, not asked: part (a)'s SVD gives σ² = 6, 2, the eigenvalues of AᵀA; ÷N gives 2, 2/3, ÷(N − 1) gives 3, 1.)

worked.title: Full PCA · Sourabh P40: PCA by hand on four points

problem.text: Points (1, 1), (2, 3), (3, 2), (4, 4); S = (1/N)X_cᵀX_c. (a) Mean and X_c. (b) S. (c) Eigenvalues and unit eigenvectors. (d) First PC, the 1-D scores, the fraction of variance. (Saurabh sir's `MFML_ZC416_Solved_Practice_Set.pdf`)

steps.label: What is tested
steps.text: The full pipeline: centre → covariance → eigen → project.

steps.label: Plan of attack
steps.text: Same five moves every time. For a 2 × 2 symmetric S, use trace and determinant for λ.

steps.label: Notation
steps.text: Saurabh sir's symbols: x̄ = mean, X_c = centred data, qᵢ = unit eigenvectors, zₙ = scores.

steps.label: STEP 3 · (c)
steps.text:
Formula: **det(S − λI) = 0**
S − λI = [[5/4 − λ, 1], [1, 5/4 − λ]]
det = (5/4 − λ)(5/4 − λ) − (1)²
    = λ² − (5/4 + 5/4)λ + 25/16 − 1
    = λ² − (5/2)λ + 9/16 = 0
    = (λ − 9/4)(λ − 1/4) = 0
⇒ **λ₁ = 9/4, λ₂ = 1/4**
Check: λ₁ + λ₂ = 5/2 = tr S ✓, λ₁λ₂ = 9/16 = det S ✓
Formula: **(S − λI)v = 0** for each λ, with v = (v₁, v₂). Solving row 1 is enough: when λ is right, row 2 gives the same line.
**λ₁ = 9/4:**
S − (9/4)I = [[−1, 1], [1, −1]]
row 1: −v₁ + v₂ = 0 ⇒ v₂ = v₁
row 2: v₁ − v₂ = 0 ⇒ the same line ✓
⇒ (1, 1); length √(1² + 1²) = √2 ⇒ **q₁ = (1, 1)/√2**
**λ₂ = 1/4:**
S − (1/4)I = [[1, 1], [1, 1]]
row 1: v₁ + v₂ = 0 ⇒ v₂ = −v₁
row 2: v₁ + v₂ = 0 ⇒ the same line ✓
⇒ (1, −1); length √(1² + (−1)²) = √2 ⇒ **q₂ = (1, −1)/√2**
Check: q₁ · q₂ = 0, perpendicular ✓

steps.label: Where marks are lost
steps.text:
• Building S from un-centred data.
• Mixing 1/N and 1/(N − 1) (state which).
• An eigenvector that is not unit length.

worked.title: Full PCA · Companion §12: five points, start to finish, with three checks

problem.text: Five points (1, 2), (4, 5), (7, 8), (8, 4), (10, 6). Reduce them from 2-D to 1-D, check the answer three ways, and project a new point (12, 9). (Saurabh sir's `Lecture_13_Companion.pdf` §12)

steps.label: What is tested
steps.text: The recipe with exact numbers, the checks Σλ = tr S and ∏λ = det S, and a new point.

steps.label: Notation
steps.text: Companion symbols: C = covariance (S on the slides), w₁, w₂ = unit eigenvectors, z = score, x̃ = reconstruction.

steps.label: STEP 6 · Three checks
steps.text:
Scores add to 0 ✓
Variance of scores = (169 + 16 + 25 + 9 + 81)/25 ÷ 5 = 300/25 = 12 = λ₁ ✓
Scores on w₂ have variance 2 = λ₂, and 12 + 2 = 14 = tr C ✓

steps.label: Where marks are lost
steps.text:

worked.title: Full PCA · Companion Q1: from raw data to components (6 marks)

problem.text: Observations (2, 3), (4, 7), (6, 5), (8, 9). (a) Mean, centred data, Σ (divide by N). [2M] (b) Eigenvalues and normalised eigenvectors. [2M] (c) First PC score of each observation; verify Var(Y₁) = λ₁; share of total variance. [2M] (Companion §15, Question 1)

steps.label: What is tested
steps.text: The five moves: mean → centre → (1/N)XᵀX → characteristic polynomial → normalise.

steps.label: Notation
steps.text: Companion question-paper symbols: Σ = covariance, α = unit direction, Y₁ = α₁ᵀX = first PC score.

steps.label: STEP 1 · (a)
steps.text:
μ = (20/4, 24/4) = (5, 6)
Centred: (−3, −3), (−1, 1), (1, −1), (3, 3)
Saurabh sir's method: **Σ = (1/N) X̂ᵀX̂**, N = 4
X̂ = [[−3, −3], [−1, 1], [1, −1], [3, 3]]   (4 × 2, one centred point per row)
X̂ᵀ = [[−3, −1, 1, 3], [−3, 1, −1, 3]]   (2 × 4: row 1 = feature 1, row 2 = feature 2)
X̂ᵀX̂: each entry = a row of X̂ᵀ times a column of X̂, multiply in pairs and add
top-left (feature 1 · feature 1) = (−3)(−3) + (−1)(−1) + (1)(1) + (3)(3) = 9 + 1 + 1 + 9 = 20
top-right (feature 1 · feature 2) = (−3)(−3) + (−1)(1) + (1)(−1) + (3)(3) = 9 − 1 − 1 + 9 = 16
bottom-left = top-right = 16 (symmetric)
bottom-right (feature 2 · feature 2) = (−3)(−3) + (1)(1) + (−1)(−1) + (3)(3) = 9 + 1 + 1 + 9 = 20
X̂ᵀX̂ = [[20, 16], [16, 20]]
Σ = (1/4)·[[20, 16], [16, 20]] = **[[5, 4], [4, 5]]**
Divide by N, not N − 1 (this course).

steps.label: STEP 2 · (b)
steps.text:
Formula: **det(Σ − λI) = 0**
Σ − λI = [[5 − λ, 4], [4, 5 − λ]]
det = (5 − λ)(5 − λ) − (4)²
    = λ² − (5 + 5)λ + 25 − 16
    = λ² − 10λ + 9 = 0
    = (λ − 9)(λ − 1) = 0
⇒ **λ₁ = 9, λ₂ = 1**
Check: λ₁ + λ₂ = 10 = tr Σ ✓, λ₁λ₂ = 9 = det Σ ✓
Formula: **(Σ − λI)v = 0** for each λ, with v = (v₁, v₂). Solving row 1 is enough: when λ is right, row 2 gives the same line.
**λ₁ = 9:**
Σ − 9I = [[−4, 4], [4, −4]]
row 1: −4v₁ + 4v₂ = 0 ⇒ v₂ = v₁
row 2: 4v₁ − 4v₂ = 0 ⇒ the same line ✓
⇒ (1, 1); length √(1² + 1²) = √2 ⇒ **α₁ = (1, 1)/√2**
**λ₂ = 1:**
Σ − I = [[4, 4], [4, 4]]
row 1: 4v₁ + 4v₂ = 0 ⇒ v₂ = −v₁
row 2: 4v₁ + 4v₂ = 0 ⇒ the same line ✓
⇒ (1, −1); length √(1² + (−1)²) = √2 ⇒ **α₂ = (1, −1)/√2**
Check: α₁ · α₂ = 0, perpendicular ✓

steps.label: STEP 3 · (c)
steps.text:
**First PC scores.** Formula: **Y₁ₙ = α₁ᵀ(xₙ − μ)**   (μ = (5, 6), α₁ = (1/√2, 1/√2))
Point 1: (2, 3) − (5, 6) = (−3, −3) ⇒ Y₁ = (1/√2)(−3) + (1/√2)(−3) = −6/√2 = **−3√2**
Point 2: (4, 7) − (5, 6) = (−1, 1) ⇒ Y₁ = (1/√2)(−1) + (1/√2)(1) = **0**
Point 3: (6, 5) − (5, 6) = (1, −1) ⇒ Y₁ = (1/√2)(1) + (1/√2)(−1) = **0**
Point 4: (8, 9) − (5, 6) = (3, 3) ⇒ Y₁ = (1/√2)(3) + (1/√2)(3) = 6/√2 = **3√2**
**Verify Var(Y₁) = λ₁:** compute the variance of these four scores directly, and check it equals λ₁ = 9 from STEP 2.
Mean of the scores: (−3√2 + 0 + 0 + 3√2)/4 = 0
Var(Y₁) = (1/N) Σ (Y₁ₙ − 0)² = ((−3√2)² + 0² + 0² + (3√2)²)/4 = (18 + 0 + 0 + 18)/4 = 36/4 = **9**
9 = λ₁ ✓ (the theory says the variance along a unit eigenvector equals its eigenvalue; this confirms it with numbers)
**Share of total variance.** Formula: **λ₁ / (λ₁ + λ₂)** = 9 / (9 + 1) = 9/10 = **90%**

worked.title: Derive · Sourabh P41: first principal component through a Lagrangian

problem.label: Notation for this solution
problem.text: **Our notation (Saurabh sir's class), used in the whole solution:** Σ → **C** (covariance), α → **w** (unit direction), Y = αᵀX → **z = wᵀX** (the projection / score), λ stays **λ**. X is the random vector.
A 2-D random vector X has covariance **Σ = [[5, 2], [2, 2]]**. The first PC is Y₁ = αᵀX with αᵀα = 1.

items: **(a)** Write the constrained problem and its Lagrangian.
**(b)** Show the stationarity condition is Σα = λα and that Var(Y₁) = λ there.
**(c)** Find α for PC1 and PC2 and their variances.
**(d)** The correlation between Y₁ and Y₂ and the share of variance of Y₁.

steps.label: What is tested
steps.text: PCA as a constrained maximum (Lagrange, Lecture 11), then solving it on numbers.

steps.label: Plan of attack
steps.text: max wᵀCw s.t. wᵀw = 1 → Lagrangian → ∂L/∂w = 0 → Cw = λw → put it back to get Var = λ → pick the largest λ → numbers.

steps.label: Notation
steps.text:
Question's letters → ours:
Σ → **C** = [[5, 2], [2, 2]] (given, so nothing to compute)
α → **w** (unit direction), Y₁ = α₁ᵀX → **z₁ = w₁ᵀX**
λ → **λ** (the Lagrange multiplier, which turns out to be the eigenvalue)
Write this mapping as the first line of your answer in the exam.

steps.label: STEP 1 · (a) Problem and Lagrangian
steps.text:
Variance of the projection: Var(z) = wᵀCw
**max wᵀCw   s.t.   wᵀw − 1 = 0**
**L(w, λ) = wᵀCw − λ(wᵀw − 1)**

steps.label: STEP 2 · (b) Stationarity
steps.text:
∂(wᵀCw)/∂w = 2Cw (C symmetric),   ∂(wᵀw)/∂w = 2w
∂L/∂w = 2Cw − 2λw = 0 ⇒ **Cw = λw**: w must be an eigenvector of C.
∂L/∂λ = 0 ⇒ wᵀw = 1 (the constraint).

steps.label: STEP 3 · (b) Var(z) = λ
steps.text:
Var(z) = wᵀCw = wᵀ(λw) = λ(wᵀw) = λ · 1 = **λ**
So to maximise the variance, take the **largest** λ.

steps.label: STEP 5 · (c) Directions and variances
steps.text:
Formula: **(C − λI)v = 0** for each λ, with v = (v₁, v₂). Solving row 1 is enough: when λ is right, row 2 gives the same line.
**λ₁ = 6:**
C − 6I = [[−1, 2], [2, −4]]
row 1: −v₁ + 2v₂ = 0 ⇒ v₁ = 2v₂
row 2: 2v₁ − 4v₂ = 0 ⇒ the same line ✓
⇒ (2, 1); length √(2² + 1²) = √5 ⇒ **w₁ = (2, 1)/√5**
**λ₂ = 1:**
C − I = [[4, 2], [2, 1]]
row 1: 4v₁ + 2v₂ = 0 ⇒ v₂ = −2v₁
row 2: 2v₁ + v₂ = 0 ⇒ the same line ✓
⇒ (1, −2); length √(1² + (−2)²) = √5 ⇒ **w₂ = (1, −2)/√5**
Check: w₁ · w₂ = 0, perpendicular ✓
**Variances.** Formula: **Var(z) = wᵀCw**. Do it in two moves: first C times w, then w dotted with that.
| Line | Working | Why |
|---|---|---|
| ① | Cw₁ = [[5, 2], [2, 2]] · (2, 1)/√5 | w₁ = (2, 1)/√5 |
| ② | = (5·2 + 2·1, 2·2 + 2·1)/√5 = (12, 6)/√5 | row 1 · (2, 1), row 2 · (2, 1) |
| ③ | w₁ᵀ(Cw₁) = (2, 1)/√5 · (12, 6)/√5 | dot w₁ with the result |
| ④ | = (2·12 + 1·6)/5 = 30/5 = **6** | √5 · √5 = 5 |
| ⑤ | Var(z₁) = 6 = **λ₁** ✓ | matches the eigenvalue |
| ⑥ | Cw₂ = (5·1 + 2·(−2), 2·1 + 2·(−2))/√5 = (1, −2)/√5 | w₂ = (1, −2)/√5 |
| ⑦ | w₂ᵀ(Cw₂) = (1·1 + (−2)(−2))/5 = 5/5 = **1** = **λ₂** ✓ | same two moves |

steps.label: STEP 6 · (d) Correlation and share
steps.text:
**Part 1 · Correlation.** Idea: correlation is 0 exactly when the covariance is 0, so find the covariance first.
Formula: **Corr(z₁, z₂) = Cov(z₁, z₂) / √(Var(z₁)·Var(z₂))**
| Line | Working | Why |
|---|---|---|
| ① | Cov(z₁, z₂) = w₁ᵀCw₂ | covariance of two projections |
| ② | = w₁ᵀ(λ₂w₂) | w₂ is an eigenvector: Cw₂ = λ₂w₂ |
| ③ | = λ₂ (w₁ᵀw₂) | λ₂ = 1 is a number, take it out |
| ④ | w₁ᵀw₂ = (1/5)(2·1 + 1·(−2)) = 0 | w₁ = (2, 1)/√5, w₂ = (1, −2)/√5 |
| ⑤ | Cov(z₁, z₂) = 1 · 0 = **0** | from ③ and ④ |
| ⑥ | Corr(z₁, z₂) = 0 / √(6 · 1) = **0** | formula above |
In words: w₁ and w₂ are perpendicular, so the covariance is 0, so the correlation is 0. This is true for **any** two principal components.
**Part 2 · Share of z₁.** Formula: **λ₁ / (λ₁ + λ₂)** = 6 / (6 + 1) = 6/7 ≈ **85.71%**

steps.label: Answers at a glance
steps.text:
L = wᵀCw − λ(wᵀw − 1); Cw = λw; Var(z) = λ
w₁ = (2, 1)/√5 with Var 6; w₂ = (1, −2)/√5 with Var 1
Correlation 0; share 85.71%
In the question's letters: α₁ = w₁, Y₁ = z₁.

steps.label: Where marks are lost
steps.text:
• Dropping the 2 on one term only (then the eigen-equation comes out wrong).
• Stopping at Cw = λw without showing Var = λ.
• Choosing the smallest eigenvalue.
• Not writing the notation mapping first.

steps.label: More
steps.text: Same Lagrange method: [Lecture 11, Lagrangian tab](#/sem1/aiml-zc416/ch11/f-lagrange/16). The full proof with data: [Type 2 board](#/sem1/aiml-zc416/ch12/lesson/5).

worked.answer: Cw = λw; w₁ (= α₁) = (2, 1)/√5 with variance 6; correlation 0; 85.71%.

worked.title: Derive · Companion Q2: find the three faults in a student's derivation (6 marks)

problem.label: Notation for this solution
problem.text: **Our notation (Saurabh sir's class), used in the whole solution:** Σ → **C** (covariance), α → **w** (unit direction), Y = αᵀX → **z = wᵀX** (the projection / score), λ stays **λ**. X is the random vector. The student's lines below are kept in their own letters; the solution answers in ours.
A student is asked to find the first principal component of a 2-D random vector X = (X₁, X₂)ᵀ with covariance **Σ = [[5, 2], [2, 8]]**, using Lagrange multipliers. Their complete attempt:

items: **(1)** Maximise Var(Y₁) = αᵀΣα subject to αᵀα = 1.
**(3)** ∂L/∂α = 2Σα − λα = 0, so Σα = ½λα.
**(5)** For the larger root, (Σ − 9I)α = 0 gives α = (1, 2)ᵀ, so Y₁ = X₁ + 2X₂.
**(6)** Var(Y₁) = 9, because the maximum variance is the largest eigenvalue.

problem.text: Exactly three of the six lines are faulty.

items: **(a)** Identify the three faulty lines and state, in one sentence each, what is wrong. [3M]
**(b)** Rewrite the derivation correctly from the first faulty line onwards, and give the correct Y₁ and Var(Y₁). [2M]

**(c)** Line (6) contradicts line (5). Compute Var(X₁ + 2X₂) directly from Σ to show this, and state the general relation between Var(αᵀX) and λ when α is an eigenvector that has not been normalised. [1M]

steps.label: What is tested
steps.text: Knowing the derivation well enough to mark someone else's.

steps.label: Notation
steps.text:
Student's letters → ours: Σ → **C** = [[5, 2], [2, 8]], α → **w**, Y₁ → **z₁ = w₁ᵀX**, λ → λ.
So the student's line (2) is L = wᵀCw − λ(wᵀw − 1) in our letters.

steps.label: STEP 1 · (a) Faults
steps.text:
Lines (1), (2) and (4) are correct. The three faults, one sentence each:
**Line (3):** the derivative of the constraint term is wrong: ∂(λwᵀw)/∂w = 2λw, not λw, so it should read 2Cw − 2λw = 0.
**Line (5):** the eigenvector is not normalised: (1, 2) is the right direction but its length is √5, and the derivation assumed wᵀw = 1.
**Line (6):** with the w of line (5) the variance is 45, not 9; Var = λ holds only for a unit eigenvector.

steps.label: STEP 2 · (b) Corrected
steps.text:
Line (3) corrected: ∂L/∂w = 2Cw − 2λw = 0 ⇒ **Cw = λw**
Line (4) stands:
Formula: **det(C − λI) = 0**
C − λI = [[5 − λ, 2], [2, 8 − λ]]
det = (5 − λ)(8 − λ) − (2)²
    = λ² − (5 + 8)λ + 40 − 4
    = λ² − 13λ + 36 = 0
    = (λ − 9)(λ − 4) = 0
⇒ **λ₁ = 9, λ₂ = 4**
Check: λ₁ + λ₂ = 13 = tr C ✓, λ₁λ₂ = 36 = det C ✓
Formula: **(C − λI)v = 0** for each λ, with v = (v₁, v₂). Solving row 1 is enough: when λ is right, row 2 gives the same line.
**λ₁ = 9:**
C − 9I = [[−4, 2], [2, −1]]
row 1: −4v₁ + 2v₂ = 0 ⇒ v₂ = 2v₁
row 2: 2v₁ − v₂ = 0 ⇒ the same line ✓
⇒ (1, 2); length √(1² + 2²) = √5 ⇒ **w₁ = (1, 2)/√5**
**λ₂ = 4:**
C − 4I = [[1, 2], [2, 4]]
row 1: v₁ + 2v₂ = 0 ⇒ v₁ = −2v₂
row 2: 2v₁ + 4v₂ = 0 ⇒ the same line ✓
⇒ (2, −1); length √(2² + (−1)²) = √5 ⇒ **w₂ = (2, −1)/√5**
Check: w₁ · w₂ = 0, perpendicular ✓
Line (5) corrected: z₁ = w₁ᵀX = **(X₁ + 2X₂)/√5**
Line (6) corrected: Var(z₁) = w₁ᵀCw₁ = λ₁(w₁ᵀw₁) = **9** (true because w₁ is unit); share 9/13 = **69.2%**

steps.label: STEP 3 · (c) Direct variance
steps.text:
Formula: **Var(aX₁ + bX₂) = a²Var(X₁) + b²Var(X₂) + 2ab·Cov(X₁, X₂)**
From C: Var(X₁) = 5, Var(X₂) = 8, Cov(X₁, X₂) = 2; here a = 1, b = 2
Var(X₁ + 2X₂) = (1)²(5) + (2)²(8) + 2(1)(2)(2) = 5 + 32 + 8 = **45**
Same in matrix form: (1, 2)C(1, 2)ᵀ = (1, 2)·(9, 18) = 9 + 36 = 45
45 ≠ 9, so line (6) contradicts line (5).
**General relation:** if Cw = λw, then Var(wᵀX) = wᵀCw = wᵀ(λw) = λ(wᵀw) = **λ‖w‖²**.
So Var = λ only when ‖w‖ = 1. Here ‖w‖² = 1² + 2² = 5, and 5 × 9 = 45 ✓

steps.label: Answers at a glance
steps.text:
Faults in lines (3), (5), (6)
z₁ = (X₁ + 2X₂)/√5 with Var(z₁) = 9; share 69.2%
Var(X₁ + 2X₂) = 45 = λ‖w‖² = 9 × 5
In the question's letters: α₁ = w₁, Y₁ = z₁.

worked.answer: Faulty lines 3, 5, 6; correct z₁ (= Y₁) = (X₁ + 2X₂)/√5 with Var 9; Var(X₁ + 2X₂) = 45.

families.title: Type 2 · Derive PCA with a Lagrangian
families.lead: Prove that the best direction is an eigenvector (Cw = λw) and that its variance is λ. Both problems here are Must do: Saurabh P41, then Companion Q2.

blocks.label: How likely (Saurabh sir, 14 Nov)
blocks.text: 70–80% chance the PCA question is a straight numerical; otherwise it is **this proof**. Last year's paper asked exactly two things: show w is an eigenvector, and show the maximum variance is λ.

blocks.label: Write this line first
blocks.text: **Assumptions:** X is N × D, one centred point per row. w is a D × 1 unit vector (wᵀw = 1). z = Xw are the projections. C = (1/N)XᵀX (divide by N, not N − 1).

groups.label: Ending 1 · w is an eigenvector
groups.note: ∂(wᵀCw)/∂w = 2Cw because C is symmetric; ∂(wᵀw)/∂w = 2w. Write **−λ** so you get Cw = λw directly.

groups.label: Ending 2 · the variance is λ
groups.note: So take the **largest** λ: PC1 is its unit eigenvector. Both endings carry marks.

blocks.text: **Always answer in w, C, z, X.** If the question uses other letters (P41 and Companion Q2 use α, Σ, Y), write one mapping line first, e.g. "Σ → C, α → w, Y → z", then solve in our letters. Never mix two notations in one answer.

blocks.label: When numbers follow the proof (P41 (c), Companion Q2 (b))
blocks.text: Same as Type 1: det(C − λI) = 0 → (C − λI)w = 0 → **unit** w → largest λ. If asked to verify Var(z₁) = λ₁: scores → mean → (1/N) Σ (z₁ₙ − mean)² = λ₁ (exam-day rule 12).

blocks.label: Where marks are lost
blocks.text: Writing λα instead of 2λα · stopping at Cw = λw without showing Var = λ · saying Var = λ for a vector that is not unit length (then Var = λ‖α‖², Companion Q2's trap) · dividing by N − 1.
Full proof with the slides' version and a side-by-side comparison: [Type 2 board](#/sem1/aiml-zc416/ch12/lesson/5).

flashcards.back: The variance of the data projected onto it (the spread of the shadows).
max bᵀSb s.t. bᵀb = 1; L = bᵀSb + λ(1 − bᵀb) ⇒ Sb = λb
λ = tr/2 ± √((tr/2)² − det); check λ₁ + λ₂ = tr, λ₁λ₂ = det
Building S from un-centred data, or giving a non-unit eigenvector.
Otherwise bᵀSb grows without limit by making b longer: only the direction should count.
S is symmetric, so its eigenvectors for different eigenvalues are orthogonal (spectral theorem).

quiz.q: Points (2, 0), (0, 2), (3, 3), (−1, −1), divide by N. Largest eigenvalue of S?
Same data: percentage of variance on PC1?
S = [[10, 4], [4, 4]]. Share of PC1 in %, to 2 decimals?
In max bᵀSb s.t. bᵀb = 1, the Lagrange multiplier at the optimum is…
quiz.explain: Sb = λb and bᵀSb = λ, so λ is the eigenvalue, the largest one for PC1.

quiz.q: Three points lie exactly on one line. The smaller eigenvalue of S is…
quiz.explain: No spread perpendicular to the line ⇒ λ₂ = 0, PC1 keeps 100%.

quiz.q: You give the eigenvector (1, 2) instead of (1, 2)/√5. Its 'variance' vᵀSv is…
quiz.explain: vᵀSv = λ‖v‖² = 5λ: that is why it must be unit length.
